summary: Builds on RFCs 3689 and 3690, which describe requirements for an Emergency Telecommunications Service, including an Internet Emergency Preparedness Service. Some such services need call preemption or queuing, and they need call admission control. This informational memo discusses how to implement those capabilities for real-time services in the IP suite.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4542 explains how IP networks can give authorized emergency calls a better chance of completing during congestion. It combines call priority, bandwidth reservations and traffic handling for real-time voice and video.

questions: how to prioritize emergency calls on ip networks
what is an emergency telecommunications service
what is the sip resource priority header
subtitle: How existing IP signaling and resource-reservation protocols can support priority calls.

tldr.problem: Emergency telecommunications may need authorized real-time calls to complete even when network capacity is constrained.
tldr.mechanism: The memo combines SIP call precedence, RSVP bandwidth admission and preemption, and Differentiated Services forwarding for voice and video.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4542 is Informational and was updated by RFC 5865. It describes an architecture using existing specifications.

today: RFC 4542 is Informational and was updated by RFC 5865. It describes how to combine existing specifications and does not define a new protocol.

sections.title: Emergency Calls on IP Networks
sections.content:
Emergency Telecommunications Service includes services that may queue calls or preempt lower-priority calls. The memo focuses on an Internet Emergency Preference Service for real-time sessions set up with SIP or H.323.

IP call control and the network paths that carry media may be managed separately. A call setup system therefore needs both permission to place a call and information about whether the network has capacity to carry it.
sections.plainLanguage: During a crisis, many people may try to call at once. The network needs a way to identify authorized calls and decide whether it can carry them.

sections.title: Precedence and Call Preemption
sections.content:
In the Multi-Level Precedence and Preemption model, a call is assigned a precedence when it starts. If capacity is scarce, a higher-precedence call may replace an existing lower-precedence call. The parties on a preempted call are notified.

The memo contrasts this with GETS, which uses two service levels and does not preempt calls; it can reserve bandwidth or queue calls instead. The proposed IP approach needs both a call precedence policy and a way to admit or preempt bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: A call carries a priority level from the start. If the network is full, policy may let a higher-priority call take capacity from a lower-priority call, and the affected users are told.

sections.title: SIP Signals Priority and Preemption
sections.content:
The SIP Resource-Priority header carries a namespace and a precedence level from the caller to the called device. A first-hop proxy can compare the requested level with the caller's authorization profile.

If a call is preempted, SIP can end it with a BYE request carrying a preemption reason. The memo's example has a user agent compare a Routine call with a later Immediate call, end the lower-priority call and accept the higher-priority one.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP carries the call's priority to the destination. The receiving phone can compare priorities and, when policy requires, end a lower-priority call before accepting a higher-priority one.

sections.title: Handling Voice and Video Traffic
sections.content:
The memo describes Differentiated Services for forwarding real-time traffic. The Expedited Forwarding behavior is intended to give voice and video enough bandwidth to keep delay variation and loss low.

Where capacity is constrained, a priority queue may be used, but traffic entering that queue needs policing to prevent abuse. The first-hop router is one suggested place to check the application's rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice and video need predictable delivery. Routers can give these packets a suitable forwarding treatment, while checking that senders do not exceed the traffic rate allowed for them.

sections.title: Reserving Bandwidth with RSVP
sections.content:
The memo recommends explicit capacity admission, with RSVP as one example. RSVP sets up one-way reservations along a path and keeps soft state that must be refreshed; the default refresh period is 30 seconds.

RSVP makes local decisions at participating devices, so every node in a network need not participate. Policy can determine whether a request is authorized and whether capacity is available. If policy admits a higher-precedence flow beyond capacity, a lower-precedence session may be torn down and the application is informed.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP asks devices along a path to reserve capacity for a call and renew that reservation periodically. Policy checks both whether the caller may request the service and whether the network can provide it.
